title_he: אַתָּה אֲדֹנִי, אוֹר לִבִּי, מְקוֹר אַהֲבָתִי

lines: אַתָּה אֲדֹנִי, אוֹר לִבִּי, מְקוֹר אַהֲבָתִי

review: The hymn is Psalm 119 stanza by stanza: 1:1–3 is Ps 119:105 with Ps 119:116 (סָמְכֵנִי כְאִמְרָתְךָ וְאֶחְיֶה), 2:1–4 is Ps 119:17–18 (גְּמֹל עַל־עַבְדְּךָ אֶחְיֶה … גַּל־עֵינַי וְאַבִּיטָה), 3:1–4 is Ps 119:19 (גֵּר אָנֹכִי בָאָרֶץ) with Lev 25:23, 4:1–4 is Ps 119:20,111 with Ps 137:4, and 5:1–4 is 2 Sam 22:29 (נֵרִי) with Ps 119:105 and 116.

Stanza 1 is three printed lines against four in the rest (3/4/4/4/4); the payload keeps three and does not pad, because the printed book sets the theme-line with its two short lines before the stanzas settle into four.

2:1 הֵיטִיבָה לִּי וְאֶחְיֶה — the Arabic رَبِّي أَحْسِنْ إِلَيَّ فَأَحْيَا is Ps 119:17's גְּמֹל עַל־עַבְדְּךָ; the Hebrew keeps the imperative plus the purpose clause, so the line asks for life as the psalm asks for it and not as a general blessing.

4:1 לְמִצְוֺתֶיךָ כָּלְתָה נַפְשִׁי — the Arabic لِوَصَايَاكَ اشْتِيَاقِي is a noun clause ('my longing is for Your commandments'); the Hebrew uses כָּלְתָה נַפְשִׁי, the psalm's own verb for consuming longing (Ps 119:81), because a Hebrew line needs a verb to carry the stanza's momentum.
